narration_full: Your Qwen isn't a mystery anymore. Every neuron inside it got mapped. You run it in Ollama or LM Studio, and when it does something weird, you shrug and re-prompt. Inside, your Qwen is a stack of identical layers. Every word it writes climbs through every layer before the next word appears. Each layer is packed with neurons, the small calculators inside it. Until now, that whole climb was invisible to you. That map is built on one rude little move. A push means adding a fixed amount to one neuron's number at every word. No prompt. No fine-tune. One number, changed. Isn't poking a neuron just brain damage? Often, yes. A verified switch is a push that changes exactly one behaviour, like which language your copy answers in. It must beat a panel of matched random neurons and keep working on questions it has never seen. Fermion Research ran that test on every neuron. Picture a mixing desk: four hundred forty-two thousand faders, one per neuron. About one fader in a hundred does one clear job. The rest do nothing you can name. One hundred thirty-two faders are verified switches. One fader is labelled German. Unpushed, it writes German seven percent of the time. Pushed a single notch, it answers in German a hundred percent of the time. A couple of notches later, it babbles. That's the limit: faders are independent and linear, neurons interact. Push past the sweet spot and the whole desk squeals. Now the honest catch, because a cute German trick is not understanding. These switches set who is speaking and how. None of them sets whether the speaker is telling the truth. The map admits what it did not find. And no, this is not a chat-party trick. The same switches still fire in the raw pretrained model. The switch-hunting framework is promised, not shipped. The atlas itself is public tonight. Your black box just grew a labelled panel. The next time Qwen does something weird, you don't re-prompt it. You look it up.

notes_for_review: Check the number discipline first: exactly three headline spends are spoken, each on its own beat — four hundred forty-two thousand faders and one hundred thirty-two switches in s05 (separate sentences), and the seven-to-a-hundred-percent German swing as one beat in s06. 'About one fader in a hundred' is spoken inside s05 only because the mandated mixing-desk analogy requires it. All other figures (36 layers, 12,288, +1.4/100, +40 vs 30 randoms, 11,079, 67/70, L5.N5224) appear as on-screen digits in the scene they belong to, per the packet amendment; the 'verified switch' definition is spoken as 'changes exactly one behaviour, beats a panel of matched random neurons, keeps working on questions it never saw' with the numeric bar on screen — confirm that satisfies the glossary. The analogy's limit is stated in s06 ('faders are independent and linear, neurons interact... the whole desk squeals') and is deliberately tied to the babbling beat, which also answers the 'you can break it 442,368 ways' half of the objection. The objection's other halves land in s07 (a cute German demo is not understanding; no truthfulness switch exists, the map admits it) and s08 (it helps tonight: atlas public, framework promised-not-shipped, switches hold in the pretrained model).
